object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Identified by account number, six digits, sequential, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six digit sequential unique identifier of an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that this account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, identified by product code. Currently three: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact / price plan that says what the customer pays and how often. Identified by plan code. Distinct from FeatureBundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- what they get, e.g. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription starts; always present, mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date... A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity, effective date, and requester. Identified by change ID.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier of a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: Date a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue, derived from price plan price normalised to a month; not stored.

source_references.excerpt: It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription

ambiguities.description: There are three distinct concepts all called 'plan': the price plan (billing artefact), the feature bundle (what the customer gets), and the sales-negotiated deal. The sales-negotiated 'plan' was explicitly deferred to another meeting and is not modeled here. Confirm no further modeling is needed for the sales deal concept.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan... and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that.

ambiguities.description: The 'one active subscription per account per product' uniqueness rule only applies to active subscriptions, but the model's Subscription fact type covers all subscriptions regardless of status. It's unclear how to formally scope the uniqueness constraint to only 'active' status subscriptions (a conditional/contextual uniqueness) versus a straightforward internal uniqueness across all subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: So it's one active subscription per account per product... No. The system blocks it.

ambiguities.description: PausedFlag is described as overlapping confusingly with SubscriptionStatus (paused subscriptions still show as active). It's unclear whether any formal constraint should govern the relationship between PausedFlag and SubscriptionStatus (e.g., exclusion or subset), or whether this is purely a known data-quality issue left unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs. prorated refund vs. credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. No constraint is modeled for refund/credit handling; this should be revisited once finance and legal decide.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Sam initially questioned whether Subscription has a single current price plan or whether it's fully derived from PlanChange history, then Priya clarified there IS a denormalised 'current plan' field maintained by the change process, with change history taking precedence if they disagree. It's ambiguous how to formally model this precedence rule (i.e., that current plan must always match the latest change) as an ORM constraint -- it's more of a derivation/consistency rule than a simple constraint type.

source_references.excerpt: No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record.
And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether Account should have Email or other identifying attributes on the 'Contact' concept mentioned in passing ('Email is on the contact, not the account'). Contact is not modeled since it wasn't elaborated, but this may be an incomplete area of the model.

source_references.excerpt: Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

ambiguities.description: Tom notes a fourth product is 'in discovery' but undefined; the ProductCode value constraint of exactly three values (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) may need to be revisited as the product set is not permanently fixed.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed at three? ... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: When an account closes and the same company returns, it is treated as a brand-new Account entity for reporting purposes, losing historical continuity. This is a known business/product tension (Tom disagrees) but no entity or relationship links a 'company' across multiple Account instances. Should there be a Company concept above Account to track this continuity, or is separate-account treatment intentional and final?

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.
Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.
